title: Fear and Medical Misinformation Regarding Risk of Progression or Recurrence Among Patients with Breast Cancer
screen_reason: Cross-sectional online survey of 997 US adults with a breast cancer history (Breastcancer.org, July-August 2023) reporting the share of respondents who encountered specific non-evidence-based claims about cancer recurrence/progression: 761 (76%) overall, 651 (65%) for risk-increasing claims, 542 (54%) for risk-decreasing claims. That is a self-reported share of respondents who encountered misinformation with a stated denominator, so it meets the RECALL inclusion criterion. The paper's association analyses (fear of recurrence, adherence) are not themselves eligible outcomes, but the descriptive exposure shares are.

estimates.platform: Online survey administered by Breastcancer.org (recruitment via site ads, Instagram, LinkedIn, Threads, Facebook and mailing list); source of the misinformation encountered was not asked
estimates.measure_type: % of breast cancer patients/survivors who reported encountering misinformation about factors purported to influence cancer progression or recurrence risk
estimates.denominator: 997 US adults diagnosed with breast cancer within the past 10 years who answered some survey questions (988, 99%, answered all misinformation items; non-answerers counted as not exposed)
estimates.definition: Respondent reported having encountered information that at least one of a fixed list of factors (judged by three clinician co-investigators to have no evidence-based association with breast cancer) increases or decreases the risk of cancer recurrence or progression.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Medical misinformation is information that is inaccurate or misleading according to the best available evidence."
estimates.n: 997 patients with a history of breast cancer
estimates.source_quote: Most participants (761 [76%]) reported encountering misinformation about factors purported to influence cancer progression or recurrence risk.
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 4 (also Abstract and Key Points)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Exposure is self-reported, so ground_truth is coded self_report per the schema rule for RECALL. But the veracity judgement was NOT the respondent's: the claim list was fixed in advance by consensus of three clinician co-investigators (M. Weiss, J. Chino, F. Chino) as factors with no evidence-based association with breast cancer, and the survey was designed by clinicians, researchers and patient advocates and pretested with patients for face validity. Respondents were asked only whether they had encountered those specific claims. No inter-rater reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Participants were presented with a list of factors commonly claimed to influence cancer recurrence or progression. They were asked whether they had encountered information that certain factors could increase (eg, sugar consumption, deodorant use, and vaccines) or decrease (eg, organic food, vitamins or supplements, and cleanses) cancer recurrence or progression risk. Three co-investigators (M.W., J.C., and F.C.) reached consensus on factors considered misinformation (ie, no evidence-based association with breast cancer).
estimates.notes: Headline row. ground_truth=self_report because the encounter is self-reported (schema rule for RECALL), but flag for the adjudicator that this instrument is stricter than the usual 'have you seen fake news?' item: the respondent never judges what counts as misinformation, they only say whether they met a specific claim from a list vetted in advance by three clinicians. If the review ever separates 'expert-anchored' from 'respondent-judged' recall items, this one belongs in the first group. breadth coded 'misleading' because the numerator includes unsupported/non-evidence-based claims (e.g. sugar, deodorant, bra type increase recurrence risk), not only demonstrably fabricated ones. population_scope is 'other': a patient population (breast cancer diagnosis within 10 years), not the general public. Self-selected convenience sample from an online breast-cancer community, 86% non-Hispanic White, 78% college-educated, no response rate reported, so the level is not population-representative.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Per-claim awareness shares were NOT given separate rows (R4, and they are single-item claims within the same instrument), but all are verbatim if an adjudicator wants them: sugar increases risk 609 (61%); deodorant 224 (22%); vaccines 78 (8%); cell phones 78 (8%); bra type 75 (8%); organic food decreases risk 409 (41%); oral vitamins or supplements 285 (29%); alkaline diet or alkalized water 121 (12%); vitamin infusions 65 (7%); essential oils 52 (5%); cleanses 51 (5%); oxygen therapy 42 (4%). (2) Fear of cancer recurrence (median FCRI-SF 19; 262 [38%] clinically significant) and self-reported treatment adherence (76%, 758 participants) are outcomes, not misinformation exposure, so no rows. The 38% vs 35% and 23% vs 26% contrasts are association tests. (3) Figures quoted from other studies are excluded per R8: 71% of surveyed survivors exposed to misinformation (ref 7), the 2018 ASCO figure that 39% of US residents believe cancer can be cured solely through alternative therapies, and the 2019 ASCO figure of 16% believing cell phones cause cancer. (4) The multivariable odds ratio for Hispanic ethnicity (aOR 2.96; 95% CI 1.15-10.05) is an association, not a share. (5) Denominator judgement call: the 76/65/54% shares are printed against N = 997, although only 988 answered all misinformation items and the 9 non-answerers were counted as NOT exposed - a small downward bias the authors state explicitly. (6) The survey did not ask where the misinformation was encountered, so platform_norm is 'survey' and no platform-specific row is possible.

rob.design: Anonymous cross-sectional online survey run by Breastcancer.org, July-August 2023, in English or Spanish; recruitment by digital ads on Breastcancer.org plus posts on Instagram, LinkedIn, Threads and Facebook and emails to the Breastcancer.org mailing list; eligible = US residents aged 18+ diagnosed with breast cancer in the past 10 years; electronic written informed consent; Solutions IRB deemed exempt; AAPOR best-practice guidelines claimed. N = 997 answered some questions, 988 (99%) answered every misinformation item and non-answerers were coded as not exposed. Self-selected convenience sample (86% non-Hispanic White, 78% college-educated or more, median age 62); no invitation denominator or response rate reported, so nonresponse bias is unquantifiable. Misinformation instrument = closed list of purported recurrence/progression factors agreed by consensus of three clinician co-investigators as having no evidence-based association with breast cancer; survey pretested with patients for face validity; no reliability statistics. FCRI-SF outcome available for only 695 (70%) of participants; complete-case analysis for the multivariable model.
rob.item6_quote: Three co-investigators (M.W., J.C., and F.C.) reached consensus on factors considered misinformation (ie, no evidence-based association with breast cancer). Participants who reported encountering these factors were considered to have been exposed to medical misinformation.
rob.item10_quote: Most participants (761 [76%]) reported encountering misinformation about factors purported to influence cancer progression or recurrence risk.
